explain.say: In deserts there are few plants to hold the ground, so strong winds easily pick up loose sand and dust.

faq.a: Yes, but mostly when it carries sand. Wind-blown grains strike rock again and again, scouring and polishing it. This is called abrasion, and it works best near the ground where the sand is.

Wind carries the most sand close to the ground, so a rock gets sandblasted most at its base. The base wears thinner than the top, making a mushroom shape. Softer rock at the bottom and water seeping in can speed this up.
A yardang is a long, streamlined ridge of rock carved by wind, pointing in the direction the wind usually blows. They can be metres to kilometres long.
When wind blows away the fine sand and dust, it leaves a tightly packed layer of pebbles behind, like a natural paved road. This protects the ground below from more wind erosion.
asks: Why are some deserts covered in pebbles?

faq.a: Yes, a lot. Rare but heavy rainstorms cause flash floods that carve canyons and move huge amounts of rock. Many desert landforms are shaped as much by water as by wind.

facts: Wind-blown sand rarely rises more than about a metre above the ground, so wind abrasion is strongest near the base of rocks.
Yardangs are streamlined ridges carved by wind and can be found on Earth and on Mars.
